paragraphs: When the first rain of summer fell on Chang’an, new curtains had just been hung in the Taiji Hall.

Fu Jian had been ill in Luoyang for two months, and still needed help to walk on the day he returned to the capital. As his procession crossed Ba Bridge, the swollen stream below ran yellow with mud, and the men bearing his litter had to rest every few steps. Fu Hong had planned to lead all the officials out to welcome him, but Fu Jian sent word to stop them: they were to carry on their business at the Department of State Affairs. There were therefore no drums of triumph along the imperial road, no new festive banners celebrating the Heavenly King’s recovery. At the city gate stood only a few laborers awaiting a review of their unpaid wages. They looked toward the distant litter before an attendant called them back into line.

As Empress Gou fastened Fu Jian’s cap, she noticed that his old belt had become loose by a notch. She called for a maid with needle and thread, but Fu Jian shook his head. “I have people to see today. Do not let them think I’ve grown so thin I cannot even keep my cap on.”
“They know how thin you’ve grown.” Empress Gou drew the jade belt tight. “I only fear you will sit too long and fall ill again after court.”

Fu Jian looked up at her. During the long nights of his illness, when he could not fully wake, he sometimes heard his attendants quietly exchanging notes on his treatment; at other times he could not even tell who was feeding him medicine. Again and again Empress Gou had sat by his bed and talked of the smallest palace affairs: someone had torn an imperial robe in the wash, a young eunuch had broken a medicine bowl, the kitchen needed more water in the rice porridge. He had thought she was trying to comfort him. Only later did he understand that she was telling him there were still living days around him, and those days did not stop when the emperor shut his eyes.
“If you begin to cough today, dismiss the court,” she said.
He agreed. Yet as he turned to leave the chamber, he looked back and said, “I may not manage that.”
Rain sounded at the end of the long corridor. Drops fell into a bronze basin beneath a stone beast’s mouth with a clear metallic ring.

The ministers prostrated themselves in welcome. Fu Rong stood beside the imperial steps and watched his elder brother climb them one at a time. He reached out several times, but Fu Jian refused his hand. Once seated, the emperor ordered the congratulatory memorials on his recovery removed. The Director of the Department had prepared a long proclamation declaring that the ancestors had blessed the dynasty and restored the Heavenly King to health. It was taken away before half the scroll had been opened.
“While I was ill, how often were the palace gates opened?” Fu Jian asked.
The Director faltered. “Officials passed through every day.”
“How many people died?”

The deputy chief censor presented the verified records of the night of fire and the forged edict, Anding, and White Horse Slope. A list of merchants ruined by the requisitions of Yao’s army was attached. Fu Jian listened carefully, told an attendant to put the records to the left of his desk, and asked, “These past months, who issued the orders?”
“The crown prince governed as regent, the Duke of Yangping assisted him, and the offices proceeded under law.”
“How many times did I wake?”
The palace physician knelt at the side of the hall. “Your Majesty was conscious by turns, then lost to us again. You could not attend continuously to affairs of state.”
“Then how did Qin go on without me?”

For a long while no one spoke. Fu Jian was not angry. He saw Fu Pi, newly come from Xiangyang, the creases still sharp in his court robe. Murong Chui stood among the generals, an unhealed injury from a bowstring on his left hand hidden within his sleeve. Beneath Fu Rong’s eyes lay dark shadows, as if he had not slept soundly for an entire season. All these men had made decisions on nights when he could not wake.
He called Fu Hong forward. “That forged edict ordered Murong Chui arrested and stripped you of the regency. Why did you refuse to obey?”
“The seal pattern was old, and the official titles were wrong.”
“What if the seals had been right?”

Fu Hong considered his answer. “The registers of orders in three offices did not agree. The palace claimed it was summoning ten thousand troops from Xiangyang, but the Department of State Affairs had no draft of the order, and the Central Army Office had no matching tally. I could act only on documents that could be verified.”
“And if I had given the order with my own mouth?”
“Father was unable to attend court then. When someone spoke on your behalf, I could not accept a reported utterance as proof of your will.”
Fu Jian regarded him for a long time. Then he ordered a question put to Fu Pi. “When you received the secret edict summoning troops, why did you not bring an army to the capital?”

Fu Pi’s face changed. In Xiangyang, men had urged him to ride north at once. They claimed the crown prince had seized control of the imperial guards, and former officers of fallen kingdoms were about to usurp the government. With a single word he could have led veterans he knew along the Han River. One night he had even put on his armor and drawn up a list of three thousand men for the vanguard. Then a deputy commander had asked: if the capital gates stayed shut, would they attack or wait? Unable to answer, he had burned the list.
“Father,” Fu Pi said, “had I brought troops home, I would not merely have been visiting my sick father. Men outside the gates would have asked if I had come to seize the throne.”
“You had no such intention.”
“But I had the troops.”

A faint rustling of sleeves passed below the imperial steps. Fu Hong did not look at his elder brother, nor did Fu Pi turn again toward the crown prince. Fu Jian ordered the forged edict brought into the hall and set beside an authentic document sent from Xiangyang. The paper was much the same color, the clay seals much alike, and the scrolls aged to just the right degree. If a clerk had not recognized the long-abolished official title, who would have dared tell the descendants of the Fu house that one of the two was false?
Fu Jian pointed to the documents. “Which seal will never fall into the hands of a wicked man?”
No one answered.

“Years ago Wang Jinglüe urged me to take back the tiger tallies. I thought that once the tallies were gathered in, I could gradually learn to make good use of every man. One illness has taught me that even my own words can be taken and used by someone else.”

An elderly imperial clansman stepped forward and urged restoration of the principle that the Heavenly King’s personal command took precedence. Military orders, he argued, could not issue through three separate gates. Give subordinates the power to return edicts with objections, and sooner or later someone would use a seal to defy the sovereign. Fu Pi agreed that on a battlefield one could not let three seal-bearing officials argue until dusk. From the other side of the hall Quan Yi spread out the forged edict. If all three seals appeared together, he said, a true catastrophe could be counterfeited. Yet fear of conspirators acting together was no reason to leave them a single door through which to enter.

Fu Jian had the Draft Provisions on the Regency and Affairs of State brought to his desk. The edges were worn from being passed among officials. As the clerk read the section on military authority, Fu Jian stopped him and asked whether a garrison commander near the capital could open a gate on receiving a secret edict. No one dared assent. He asked next whether, if illness sent him into another two months of unconsciousness and a lone palace attendant emerged carrying an edict, the crown prince ought to obey it. Fu Hong stood beneath the steps without looking at his father. Those who had stopped the false edict beyond the sickroom knew the question had not been posed to them for an easy answer.

The clerk went on. To move capital troops, seals or tallies from three offices were required. To wage a campaign beyond the frontier, the edict must be drafted and verified again. On grave punishments or large-scale population transfers, the Department of State Affairs could submit a signed objection. If fighting suddenly broke out at the border, commanders could first protect the territory under attack, but must report within three days and could not use an emergency as a pretext to march on the capital. When the clerk reached the provision on succession, Fu Jian himself took up the brush. Physicians, members of the imperial clan and the civil officials must jointly verify the ruler’s death; a secret edict from the bedchamber alone could not settle the inheritance of the throne. He signed at the foot of the document. The brush paused, leaving a dense black dot.
At this, the old minister bowed twice. “I cannot agree. The Heavenly King possesses all under Heaven. How can a petty official, with a mere written objection, stand in his way?”

Fu Jian asked him to rise and replied with a question. “When fire broke out in Chang’an and the forged edict came, the people who stopped it were minor clerks. If you had been guarding the palace gate that night, would you have opened it?”
The old man’s face flushed. At last he answered, “I too would have needed to examine the evidence.”
“Then let those who come after us examine it as well.”

Once the draft was circulated, the military administration still found provisions that would be difficult to apply. Fu Pi pointed out that if the relay roads flooded, a report within three days might be impossible. Murong Chui asked who could truly stop the Heavenly King if, knowing the officials objected, he persisted with a mistaken order. Fu Jian made no pretense that the text could solve everything. He told the clerk to add a requirement for proof of road conditions when a late report was defended, and retained the procedures for a compelled second deliberation and a signed record of responsibility. As to who could stop every ruler who made a mistake, he gave no answer.

“Those who draft laws always hope their words will be free of flaws for ten thousand years,” Fu Rong said. “Yet for every order you have issued these past years, the men below have managed to discover ten fresh difficulties.”
“Then leave those ten difficulties in the record,” Fu Jian said.
The ministers had expected a gracious assembly to celebrate the ruler’s recovery. Instead, before court was dismissed, the first dispute had already turned upon the Heavenly King himself.

An urgent report arrived from Beidi. After Yao Chang’s death, a band of his remaining followers had crossed the mountains and stolen horses. Several Qiang households in three nearby counties had secretly supplied dried grass and weapons. On hearing this, Fu Jian immediately ordered the Qiang households of all three counties gathered and moved into the prefectural city, so that the rebels would lose their support. Invoking the new provisions, the Director of State Affairs asked him to suspend the order and first arrest those implicated, establishing who had furnished horses and who had provided grain. Fu Jian’s expression darkened.
“If we wait until they run before chasing them, when will we ever catch them?”

“Twenty thousand people would have to be escorted. There will be no one to harvest the autumn grain or weave winter clothes.” The Director knelt, sweat gathering along his temples. “I dare not affix the seal.”
Fu Jian stared at him. “You mean to use the words I spoke just now to obstruct me?”
“I am acting upon the words Your Majesty spoke just now.”

The palace fell utterly silent. Outside the rain had not stopped, and a shallow pool was forming before the threshold. Fu Rong stepped forward and asked whether the Director would sign his reasons for returning the edict. The Director said he would, and remained kneeling as he wrote them out item by item. The general who held the Central Army Office seal also said that a mass transfer would consume troops needed to pursue the rebels. He proposed sealing the mountain routes and searching for ten days, with no transfer for the moment. The Court of Justice had evidence of three households supplying horses. It was not enough to establish treasonous intent throughout three counties.

Looking at the three opinions, Fu Jian suddenly remembered the proclamation at White Grass Valley. Yao Chang had claimed the court would sooner or later condemn all Qiang as rebels. If twenty thousand Qiang were marched away today, what would their elders and children remember afterward? That something the dead Yao Chang had said had come true.
He put the population-transfer edict back on the desk. After a long time he asked, “Who will pursue them?”
“Your younger brother will go,” Fu Rong said. “We shall seal the mountain routes first, and leave the houses of the innocent untouched.”
“And if you have caught no one in ten days?”
“We shall examine the evidence again.”

Fu Jian fell silent. At last he ordered a new military directive drafted: the Beidi command was to arrest the remnants at the mountain passes, detain those who aided them only on evidence of their actual acts, and inspect village horses without confiscating them under that pretext. The discarded transfer edict was not to be destroyed. It would be sealed in the archive together with the Director’s written objection.
“Your Majesty, if the order was never carried out, why preserve it?” someone asked.
Fu Jian leaned against the throne and coughed twice. “It bore my name. Keep it, so that those who come afterward will know how close it came to passing the palace gate.”

The council did not break up until afternoon. Fu Jian kept his two sons, Fu Rong and Murong Chui behind. Only when the hall emptied did Fu Pi voice what he had held back. “Father, if you had insisted on moving those households, what could the offices have done?”
“They could have urged me again.”
“And if they failed?”
“Then someone would have had to write plainly in the record who made the decision.”
Fu Pi said this would never do in battle. Murong Chui nodded. “Not in battle, certainly. But the decision to dispatch ten thousand men is made before the army reaches the battlefield.”
Fu Pi turned to him. “What if you had been at the Fei River, waiting for all three seals while the Jin army crossed ahead of you?”

“We did not fight at that river because we had first discovered that our grain wagons were still behind us,” Murong Chui answered. “If enemy horsemen had truly ridden into the camp, I would have drawn my sword. And afterward, if the court summoned me to answer, I would have answered.”

Fu Pi was silent. Fu Hong handed the key to the regent’s seal chest to the Director of State Affairs. During the two months when his father could not speak, that seal had kept many palace gates from being opened recklessly; now it belonged back in storage. He set the key on the wooden desk, but for a long time his fingers did not release it.
“Reluctant to let go?” Fu Jian asked.
“I am,” Fu Hong said, raising his head. “At last I know the weight of a matter entrusted to one’s hands. And I know that if I misstep, people will always say the crown prince did it deliberately.”

Fu Jian nodded and did not ask him to say more. Father and son stood on opposite sides of the desk while the rain outside diminished. Fu Rong took Murong Chui and Fu Pi away. At the door he glanced back quietly: Fu Jian had reached to steady the seal chest, while Fu Hong still held his head low. Many years earlier, at Wang Meng’s sickbed, the dying minister had asked the Heavenly King to bring the crown prince into the Department of State Affairs. Neither father nor son had then understood where that order might lead.

Ten days later the provisions were promulgated, and three original copies sealed away in separate places. No one dared claim forged edicts would now disappear. Men in Chang’an prison would still sell false warrants for profit, and documents would still go missing on distant relay roads. Replacing one seal with three had not made the hard matters fewer. It had merely made it possible to ask who was responsible at each point.

The first small difficulty concerned wages owed to river-granary laborers. Fu Jian read a memorial requesting the return of wages to thirty-one households, and as usual wrote, “Approved.” But a young clerk did not take the document to be sealed. He said the expenditure office must first check its old accounts. Fu Jian asked, “Must even this wait?”
“If the wages are not properly checked, the county may pay too much or too little.”
“How long?”
“Before noon tomorrow.”

Fu Jian looked at the wage list, so creased it was almost translucent. It bore his own name, and the names of thirty-one households that had waited a year. Gently he put the seal back in its chest. “Send it for checking.”

The following day the expenditure office discovered that one household had already received half the wages the previous year, while another name had been copied incorrectly. Only after the records were amended was the balance paid. When the clerk brought the papers back, Fu Jian added a single character beside his approval: “Verified.” He did not scold the young man for needless trouble again.

At dusk Fu Hong brought the last old files from his regency. Fu Jian sat propped against his bed, his complexion still poor despite his recovery. He asked the crown prince to sit and said, “Yao Chang asked why Qin still bears the name of Fu. Have you thought about that?”
Fu Hong laid the case papers down. “I have.”
“Have you an answer?”
“Not yet.”

“Neither have I.” Fu Jian looked out the window. “We can begin by reviewing the annual stipends paid to imperial kinsmen. Titles may remain hereditary, but stipends need not remain unchanged for every generation. No one guilty of a crime should escape punishment for bearing the Fu surname. Draft the proposals yourself, and take your time. Do not say that because Yao Chang is dead, the question he raised has died with him.”

Fu Hong agreed. As he was about to leave, he heard his father softly call, “Jinglüe.” Thinking he had misheard, he stopped. But when he turned, Fu Jian’s eyes were already closed. Fu Hong drew the curtain over him without disturbing the palace physician.

The lamps in the Taiji Hall gradually dimmed, while the Department of State Affairs remained bright. Someone there was checking relay reports of the Yellow River’s rising waters; another was copying the balances of the Luoyang granaries; someone else was searching the old military register for the husband of a woman from a distant county. After the rain stopped, a night watchman walked along the corridor and heard through a window the soft rustle of pages being turned.
